title: Wallpaper Groups — rich
forward_vector: I am the manifest of Wallpaper Groups' rich face, its first round at Sketch tier: three made pieces that each walk up to a test the page's own text sets (which turns a lattice can hold and how the seventeen really split, one tile put through all seventeen against the kaleidoscope sentence, and a two-voice loop put to the rhythmic impossibility sentence), and the May p4m cell laid beside the Alhambra, with the fingerprint of the words each was laid against and the offers the pieces measured for the text. I grow when a piece has something new to test; I never hold the entry's words.

offers.what: The list's counts are wrong for its labels, and its first line names one group under "4". Counted on the which-turns piece's engine, the section's own four kinds hold 1 (p1), 3 (pm, pg, cm), 4 (p2, p3, p4, p6) and 9 (pmm, pmg, pgg, cmm, p4m, p4g, p3m1, p31m, p6m), not 4, 5, 3, 5; read with glides as reflections, the only reading that fills all four bins. By highest turn the split is 4, 5, 3, 3, 2 (none, half, third, quarter, sixth); the page's 4, 5, 3, 5 is that split with two bins merged, quarter + sixth or third + sixth (the hexagonal family), and the count alone can't tell which. Proposed: "1 with translation only (p1); 3 with reflection or glide and no turn (pm, pg, cm); 4 with turns and no reflection (p2, p3, p4, p6); 9 that mix turns with mirrors or glides." Or split by turn into five lines: none 4, half 5, third 3, quarter 3, sixth 2.

"Rotate the central fragment, and the entire pattern rotates in lockstep" holds only in the 5 groups with no reflection (p1, p2, p3, p4, p6). Measured on the one-tile piece's engine: turn the tile 0.3 rad and every unreflected copy turns +0.3, every reflected copy −0.3, in all 12 groups with a mirror or glide, exactly half the copies each; and no copy's centre moves, so the pattern as a whole never turns. A kaleidoscope is made of mirrors (three in a triangle give p3m1, p4m or p6m), so it is one of the 12. Proposed: "Turn the central fragment and every copy turns with it, the mirrored ones the other way: the pattern changes, and its symmetry holds."

"In 1985, crystallographer M.C. Escher and mathematician H.S.M. Coxeter established … all 17" is wrong, not just unsourced. Escher was a graphic artist, not a crystallographer, and died on 27 March 1972; he visited the Alhambra in 1922 and May–June 1936 and copied its tilings, and met Coxeter at the 1954 ICM in Amsterdam; no 1985 count by either exists. The record: Müller's 1944 Zürich thesis counted 12 per Grünbaum (Notices of the AMS 53:6, June/July 2006), 11 per Bodner (Bridges 2013); Grünbaum found her twelve plus one on his 1983 visit; Grünbaum, Grünbaum and Shephard (1986) found at most 13, missing p2, pg, pgg and p3m1; Pérez-Gómez (Comput. Math. Appl. 14, 1987) and Montesinos (Classical Tessellations and Three-Manifolds, Springer 1987) claimed all 17; Grünbaum (2006) disputed that, objecting to colour, interlace and inconsistent criteria; Bodner (2013) found 14, missing p2, pmg and p3m1, excluding a single tile as not a tiling, and notes all 17 occur in Islamic ornament worldwide but not shown at one site. Proposed: "Whether all 17 are there is still argued: Müller counted 12 in 1944, Montesinos claimed all 17 in 1987, Grünbaum disputed it in 2006, and Bodner found 14 in 2013." The section's "Not mostly. Not about. All 17.", its next paragraph, and the forward vector's "encoded all 17" lean on the contested count. Sources: faculty.washington.edu/moishe/branko/BG262.Alhambra.pdf; sites.uwm.edu/ancel/files/2017/04/Bodner.Planar-Crystallographic-Groups-Represtented-at-the-Alhambra.2013-xsue3q.pdf.

offers.section: Musical Symmetry: Rhythm as Wallpaper Group
offers.what: The rhythmic impossibility sentence holds in a 16-step bar and fails in other loops. Measured on the rhythm piece's engine: in 16 steps a fifth of a turn is 3.2 steps, and five cells of 3 leave a 1-step gap, five of 4 overlap by 4, neither five-fold; in 15 steps (cells of 3) or 20 (cells of 4) there is no gap, no overlap, and the loop is five-fold. Every k from 2 to 12 fits a loop of 2k steps. On a timeline a turn of the loop is a slide in time, and the limit is that k divides the loop's length: arithmetic, not geometry, and no turn is forbidden outright. Off the grid it always fits: five quintuplets in a 4/4 bar are five-fold. The line's real shadow of the restriction is stricter and different: a line's only point symmetries are the identity and the reversal, which is why a strip has 7 groups (the piece's steps 2 and 3 show it). Proposed: "The crystallographic restriction has a musical shadow, but a softer one: on a step grid a loop can be five-fold only if five divides its length. A 16-step grid can't hold it; a 15- or 20-step loop can."

offers.section: Musical Symmetry: Rhythm as Wallpaper Group
offers.what: The page means this literally: "is a wallpaper group in time" (line 77), "The mathematics is identical" (line 85), "This is not a metaphor" (line 34). A repeating rhythm is a strip, not a plane: time runs along it, the voices across it, and it repeats in one direction only. Its symmetries are the 7 frieze groups, not the 17 wallpaper groups; random two-voice loops on the rhythm piece's engine reach exactly the seven (p1, p11g, p11m, p1m1, p2, p2mg, p2mm). On one voice, a half-turn and a mirror in time make the same loop (all 256 first halves of a 16-step loop). The glide is also misplaced: kick-snare-kick-snare is itself p2mg, its glide one beat along with low and high swapped; the section puts the glide in the quarter-note hi-hat instead. Proposed: "A repeating rhythm is a frieze group in time, one of seven …" with the glide example moved to the kick-snare. Caveat: pitch against time, with a sequence that transposes as it repeats, is periodic in two directions, so wallpaper groups do reach music there; rhythm alone is a frieze.

offers.section: Musical Symmetry: Rhythm as Wallpaper Group
offers.what: Aimed at the bundle's recipe-p2, recorded here because the rhythm piece measured it: its rule, "a hit at position n maps to position (n + 8) mod 16", is a slide, not a 180° turn. On a cell with no symmetry of its own it makes p1 (hop), with no half-turn. On one line a true half-turn is the reversal n → 17 − n, which is recipe-pm's mirror; p2 and pm come apart only with a second voice (the piece's two-voice step: half-turn reverses and swaps the voices, making p2).

offers.section: Wallpaper Groups in World Music — An Initial Mapping
offers.what: The Ewe bell is named E(5,12) but its accents, 1, 3, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, are seven: checked on the rhythm piece's engine, the list is E(7,12) turned (Toussaint's standard bell), not E(5,12). The same check finds the listed pattern doesn't land on itself under a third of a turn (4 steps), so it has no three-fold skeleton of its own; the "is p3" line may want a second look when the section is next worked.

Seen in passing, not tested by a piece: "the Shubnikov groups (double groups)". Shubnikov (Heesch–Shubnikov) groups are the black-and-white (antisymmetry, magnetic) groups, where an operation may also swap two colours; in the plane there are 80 (17 ordinary, 17 grey, 46 two-colour). Double groups (Bethe 1929) extend point groups for half-integer spin, a different construction. The parenthesis wants "black-and-white groups". The bullet's "color-preserving operations" fights its own "anti-symmetries where color reverses"; and the colour swap is time reversal in the magnetic groups, so the next bullet, "Time-reversal symmetry", is the same thing split off. Müller's 1944 thesis also studied these 80 (Grünbaum 2006, footnote 3).

offers.section: Musical Symmetry: Rhythm as Wallpaper Group
offers.what: From the challenger: "Polyrhythms (2 against 3, 5 against 7) are incommensurate periodicities" (line 81) is wrong. Both ratios are rational: 2 against 3 repeats every 6 subdivisions, 5 against 7 every 35, as line 79's own least common multiple says. The Lissajous comparison (never closing) holds only for irrational ratios. Proposed: "commensurate periodicities that realign every 6 (or 35) subdivisions; only an irrational ratio never closes."

From the challenger: the page says every tiling in nature and every crystal falls in the 17 or the 230 (lines 34, 40 "Nature enforces this", 63). Quasicrystals are crystals under the IUCr's 1992 definition: ordered, not periodic, with five-fold or icosahedral symmetry, and found in nature (icosahedrite, Khatyrka meteorite). Lu and Steinhardt (Science, 2007) found quasi-periodic girih tilings at the Darb-i Imam shrine, Isfahan, 1453: the same craft tradition stepped past the periodic limit. Proposed: scope the claims to periodic patterns and crystals, and name quasicrystals as the open door; a later piece setting "Nature enforces this" beside a Penrose tiling would be a test.

verdicts.why: A test: a real proof of the restriction (2·cos(360°/n) whole), then a count of the seventeen that could have gone either way and shows the section's 4, 5, 3, 5 is wrong for its labels (1, 3, 4, 9); walks up from one quarter-turn. Note: the 4, 5, 3, 5 also fits none / half / square family / hexagonal family, so the verdict line could name both merges.

pieces.title: which turns fit · five steps
pieces.caption: **Which turns can a repeating pattern hold?** A square lattice turned until its points land, then any turn on square and hexagonal lattices, then the fifth-turn: pentagons leave 36° or overlap 72°, and a set closed under a fifth-turn has no shortest step (0.382, 0.236, 0.146, each the golden ratio smaller). The test: 2·cos(360°/n) must be whole, so n is 1, 2, 3, 4 or 6. Last, the seventeen from one tile, sorted. By the section's own kinds they count 1, 3, 4, 9, not 4, 5, 3, 5; the section's numbers are the split by highest turn (4, 5, 3, 3, 2) with two bins merged, and the count can't tell which two. Checked in Node on the piece's own engine.

verdicts.why: Caption only: the comma is mirror-symmetric about its own diagonal, so it sits on a p4m mirror and the sheet shows four copies per cell, not "eight copies"; rewrite that clause (wording in the challenge record) and keep the Bodner/Lindaraja and p6m lines, both checked.

pieces.title: one p4m cell · the May 2026 proofs
pieces.caption: One p4m cell. The comma is itself symmetric about a diagonal, so it sits on a mirror and shows four times per cell, not the eight a general motif would. Four-fold centres lie on the mirrors. Bodner (2013) photographs a p4m tile dado in the Mirador de Lindaraja. The sheet's own line calls p4m the most symmetric group; p6m is, with twelve copies to p4m's eight.

verdicts.why: A real test that bites (five-fold fails in 16, fits in 15 and 20), walks up from one cell, silent until a click, stops on step change, suspended when hidden. Note: "in a 16-step bar the section is right" holds only on the grid (quintuplets are five-fold in 4/4); say grid.

pieces.title: rhythm on a strip · five steps
pieces.caption: **Rhythm on a strip.** One looped cell; then sixteen steps whose second half is made from the first, where on one line backwards and half-turn give the same loop; then a second voice, where they part and the loop reads as one of the seven frieze groups (kick-snare-kick-snare is p2mg, a glide); then the loop as a clock, where a 1/k turn is a slide of n/k steps. The test: five-fold on a 16-step grid leaves a gap or overlaps, as the section says, and in 15 or 20 steps it fits and plays. The bundle's recipes can be tried here: write the half, choose the fill. Checked in Node on the piece's own engine; the mix was not heard.

verdicts.why: Walks up from the tile alone to all seventeen and tests the kaleidoscope sentence: in the 12 groups with a mirror or glide exactly half the copies counter-turn (an index-2 subgroup), 5 turn in lockstep. Note: "no copy's centre moves" is the piece's construction, not a finding; the mirrors-stay-put line is the honest form.

pieces.title: one tile · six steps
pieces.caption: **One tile, and only the operations change.** The tile alone; slid into p1; turned into p2, p3, p4, p6; reflected into pm, pg, cm; then the nine that combine, with their mirrors, glides and turn centres shown. The test: all seventeen from the one tile, turning together. Nothing is added but operations, as the section says. The kaleidoscope sentence holds in the five groups with no reflection; in the other twelve, half the copies turn the other way, and the pattern as a whole never turns.
